title: Polymorphism
description: Compile-time vs. runtime polymorphism, dynamic method dispatch, and upcasting/downcasting.
objectives: Distinguish compile-time polymorphism (overloading) from runtime polymorphism (overriding)

content.heading: Compile-Time vs. Runtime Polymorphism
content.body: Java has two forms of polymorphism ('many forms'). Compile-time polymorphism (also called static binding) is method overloading: the compiler decides, at compile time, which overload to call based purely on the declared types of the arguments at the call site. Runtime polymorphism (dynamic binding) is method overriding: which overridden method actually runs is decided at runtime, based on the object's actual, real type — not the type of the reference variable pointing to it.

content.heading: Dynamic Method Dispatch and Casting
content.body:
This is best seen through a superclass reference holding a subclass object: Animal a = new Dog(); a.speak();. Even though a is declared as type Animal, calling a.speak() runs Dog's overridden speak() — the JVM looks at the object's actual runtime type to decide which version to invoke, called dynamic method dispatch. This is what makes polymorphism useful in practice: code written against a common supertype (Shape, Animal, Payable) automatically works correctly with any subclass, without needing to know which specific subclass it's dealing with.

Upcasting (Animal a = new Dog();) is implicit and safe, since a Dog genuinely is an Animal. Downcasting (Dog d = (Dog) a;) is required to access members that exist only on the subclass, and is only safe if a's actual runtime object really is a Dog (or a further subclass) — check with instanceof first to avoid a ClassCastException.

content.explanation: Even though the array's declared element type is Shape, each s.area() call dispatches to that specific object's own overridden implementation — Circle's or Square's — determined at runtime by the object's real type.

keyPoints: Overloading is resolved at compile time (based on argument types); overriding is resolved at runtime (based on the object's actual type)
A superclass reference can hold a subclass object; calling an overridden method dispatches to the subclass's version
Upcasting is implicit and always safe; downcasting requires an explicit cast and can fail at runtime
instanceof lets you safely check an object's actual type before downcasting
commonMistakes: Assuming a superclass-typed reference calling a method runs the superclass's version (it runs the actual object's overridden version)
Downcasting without checking instanceof first, risking a ClassCastException
Confusing overloading (compile-time, based on declared argument types) with overriding (runtime, based on actual object type)
